evidence: Main tools/swarm/swarmctl_hardening_base.py transition_check() compares immutable event bytes only between the supplied immediate before/after snapshots; it does not anchor event history to the last validated state or an immutable digest chain.

Control commit ebc699fc416346e5a6dc6cc02f6d992b635f205f normalized evt-20260811-080520-h4v8n2-cart-geometry-review.json. Run 31472270118 proved the after snapshot is structurally PASS, then failed only because transition-check detected that exact event path changed from immediate parent 54b28d6e6cd9de972cc63801a50b33a9ba0299dd.

swarm-control is not branch-protected, so the red mutation commit remains the authoritative parent for later pushes. On a descendant that leaves the normalized event bytes unchanged, the present transition_check() computes be[k] == ae[k] for that path and cannot detect that the mutation was never validated.

render() creates validation.json from only the current stateDigest after current transition success; no historical event digest/validated ancestor is included. A later successful descendant can therefore publish a PASS marker over the previously rewritten event bytes.

recentEvents.summary: Swarm immutable-event enforcement is only one-transition deep and can launder a forbidden historical-event rewrite through one red control commit. A commit that mutates an existing event correctly fails transition-check, but because swarm-control itself accepts that red commit as the new branch tip, the next unrelated commit compares against the already-mutated parent. If it leaves that event unchanged, transition-check sees no change and can render a fresh validation marker whose state digest now trusts the rewritten event history. This violates the append-only event authority model and must be repaired before treating validation-fence recovery as durable.
